It's like an indie film, like really indie, 2 guys with a camcorder in the wood indie, turned into a ps1 horror game. It's weird and janky and genuine and empathetic and REAL. It clearly has its influences, Alan Wake, Twin Peaks, Silent Hill, ect, but it comes together into something all its own. The real delight is the cutscenes, shot like a real film as much as possible, despite clearly limited animation and budget (though some of the choices to look this way are surely intentional, the photograph faces never stop being mesmerizing). In its best moments the strange photographs plastered onto low polygon models and surfaces aesthetic creates truly beautiful and surreal images. 

I don't know if I just don't know how people from Appalachia talk, or if the dialog is weird and dreamlike in an effort to be similar to silent hill, but it's SO strange. The leads especially seem to always use like, just the wrong word. I was always wondering what nuts thing they would say next. Some of the writing in the inventory items of all things is absolutely fantastic. There's a packet of beef jerky that in the menu contains the script for an entire Superbowl commercial for the product that had me cackling.

As a "game" it's largely o-kay. I'm a little baffled by there being no option for non-tank controls but that's a personal preference. The bulk section of the game has you navigating a maze like forest and amusement park sort of rubbing around for key items to build a bridge or open a locked door, and I would say they make you circle that place about 2 times too many, feels like padding. There's no combat, so there's no real tension to most of the exploration (danger is limited to scripted chase sequences) so I could have either used less wandering around or let me move much faster, or for the areas to be smaller. (I know there are plot reasons the guy can't run for too long but man, I hate that he gets tired during normal exploration)

Overall if you're a fan of weird, unique art that wears it's heart on its sleeve this is highly recommended. My jaw was on the floor during some of these story beats. It's also far more mature in a real way than it first appears (the family trauma stuff is painful, complimentary). The best parts are when the 2 heroes are just bullshitting about life and the game knows it. Love this, hope they make more games!

[h2]Everything I hoped for from their DEMO[/h2]
Am I a super-fan? Nah, I just want to give creators, particularly those who put a lot of effort and individuality into the worlds and characters they create the praise that they deserve. 10 DEAD DOVES isn't necessarily a horror game. It's more of a thrilling atmospheric walking simulator, with a few subpar (but enjoyable) jump scares and whisper / shadows. 

If you're anticipating this game to be terrifying, you'll be disappointed. It's a highly emotional narrative of Sean and Mark's adventure through the Appalachian Ant Farm, where an urban legend has grown as a result of the numerous disappearance of hikers and campers in the area. The narration is the most compelling selling point because it feels authentic. It doesn't feel too mushy or fake due to fantasy; it's as if the creators got up behind the mics and played themselves not a character. 

Using high-fidelity images, similar to but superior to Half Life, or I suppose you could use PS1 graphics as an example. The game takes on a completely unique graphical appearance you won't see anywhere else with facial expressions. Everything appears to be decently done, as if the developer attempted something but made a mistake and, rather than rebuilding it, simply went with what they had and made it their own. 

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
In short, it's a masterpiece because of how they portray the experience and their mutual support. The understanding between you and the main character emotionally, as well as the fact that everything looks amazing thanks to the distinctive high fidelity visual surreal style. 

If you enjoy long and drawn-out exploration, various choices, and branched endings where your decisions have an influence and there are many things that can be overlooked and pieced together, then 10 DEAD DOVES will undoubtedly appeal to you. That being said, if all you're looking for is cheap jumpscare horror or anything approximating the current horror cliche, this is more suited to fans of vintage Silent Hill. It is a walking simulator, not a fighting game.

so, I wasn't not entertained, but I gotta say, this game falls somewhere between like YIIK & Concluse 2 on the scale of games that try and miss the mark, and also way overdo it. 

honestly this ends up mostly incoherent and fails to really tell much of a story; very often it felt like things just kinda happened. often I would make a joke about what was about to happen and I kept being right (eg: collect my 8 pages mark, then it actually was a slender section where you need to collect 10. or the time I said "and now for the musical number" and then a character like a minute later starts singing). so the yiik bones come from a lot of the references shoved in here and just how a lot of it seems to be being weird for the heck of it. I will say it does a better job than that game, but like, I still felt like I was playing that without a long monologue stopping gameplay for a while (instead it was long dialogues). so the concluse 2 bones come from how much this game starts to overstay its welcome and how much you seem to just get thrown into another weird confusing situation all the time and you can like barely piece it together. like you start off en media res and it takes like hours for you to figure out what they're even doing in the woods or like what's going on with the dreams, and by the end you're still confused because a lot of it goes without answer and not really enough info to figure it out. and like both games I'm comparing it to, weird shit just seems to kinda happen for its own sake.

so the story structure is of course very odd and doesnt help, they don't really establish who the characters are or their motivations for a while, some are still sort of vague, if not for the nonsense, you would stop from not caring about what's happening. a lot of the dialogue, especially early on, felt very disjointed, like one character would say something and the other character would sort of go off about something else, like one of the car conversations just felt off, like it wasn't a conversation. the plot itself felt like it just kinda slinked along and felt a bit slapdash and cobbled together from a bunch of different plot threads that only sort of matched up. a lot of side notes and lore or whatever felt like they didn't provide new info and instead would a lot of the time tell stuff I could already infer just from like the environment and what happened already in the story. I feel like the vision mechanic added nothing but furthered confusion, just more out of context bits.

game has bad audio mixing on dialogue and a lot of it is quiet, but subtitles work.

the gameplay was fine, it's more like an adventure game than anything. major complaint is what the hell is going on with the sprint? the character would without pressing anything just go into sprint speed, but then also slow down a ton a lot. just strange and inconsistent move speed. now during the few chase segments, sometimes the character would not move fast, just walk, and I'd have to go back to a checkpoint. there's also the trash pickup option which seemed like an achievement thing but this game has no achievements, so it's pointless.

but yeah I was entertained, but this game is not without its problems. I dont recommend playing it all at once either, not like it matters a ton cause you're gonna be confused either way.

There were definitely times that I felt this game overstayed its welcome, but yet I couldn't put it down. It's 4 AM and I'm just now finishing it and god, I'm glad I did.

To compare it to the works its obviously inspired by (David Lynch's catalogue, Control, Portal, Half Life, Resident Evil, PT...the list goes on) is a disservice. 10 Dead Doves blends all of these into a truly compelling, forward-driven narrative that kept me going, even through tanky controls and at times dark and frustrating level design. 

The animation is one aspect I really want to point out: being incredibly cinematic but yet, unrealistic, retro-styled. At times, it literally felt like I was watching a blockbuster movie and not cutscenes in a video game with the artful pacing, framing, and smooth, bespoke animations themselves.

It is a story of love, of loss, of fear, of government boogeymen and scary monsters in the woods and a broken marriage and a rocky friendship. It's a story of introspection, of confrontation, of conquest and defeat in every meaning of the words. Everyone can relate to the rich cast of characters in some way: whether the compulsive Wren or the jovial Sean, or the innocent Charlie, caught up in a situation she didn't ask for.

Absolutely fantastic work.

I backed this on Kickstarter and am giving it a positive review for the ambition with a few large caveats.

Firstly, having only tank controls was so annoying. I hate tank controls, and even though I got used to it over time, they still felt awkward and terrible.

The gameplay is a mixed bag and mostly involves walking around and discovering items to progress with minimal puzzles involved. There is a tedious amount of searching areas for specific components of items that frequently requires backtracking. There is some reward for this, as the game switches up angles and areas a bit when you have to backtrack, but not necessarily enough to overcome the tedium. Collecting six planks of wood to build a bridge is not particularly enthralling game design.

The sound mix on the voices is horrendous. I do not understand how they produced such poor quality audio, as the mixing was all over the place. Sometimes the voices were too soft, other times too loud, and the voice acting was, charitably, mediocre, with the actors frequently seeming to mumble into their microphones rather than actually talk. I ended up keeping the voice volume at 100% and turned sound effects and music to 50% while raising my computer volume just to get a better mix of the voices with the music and sound. There is little excuse for this, as many other indie games have managed to have better acted and mixed audio with a similar production value. You don't get points for effort, just the result.

The story is....

Very abstract. This is highly subjective, of course, but I felt like the disparate elements didn't quite gel in an emotionally satisfying way at the end of the game. I cottoned to what was happening for the most part, but everything was so bizarrely distended and distorted with little narrative cohesion that it strained my desire to see it through to completion. It wasn't a bad journey, per se, but it was a bit unfulfilling. This felt very much like the creators wanted a Lynchian story, but didn't have the polish or emotional depth to pull off their ambitions.

That's not to say this is all middling. The lo-fi graphics are put to good use here and the art style can occasionally be really inspired, with the unique facial animations and stitched-together art graphics looking not quite like anything I've seen before in a game. That was what propelled me forward through much of the title's runtime, and the relationship between Sean and Mark was compelling enough to keep me engaged (I wish there was more of that, to be honest).

The devs here swung for the fences, and while they faltered in many technical and narrative aspects (the sound mix and voices chief among them), I admire the tenacity and desire to create something really weird and unique. I hope they take whatever real and valid criticisms come from this and make something next that fulfills its own promise and truly shines.

If you're scrolling through games looking for your next quick fixation - something interesting, something surprising, something to chew on - stop here. 10 Dead Doves is *kind* of funny. It's *kind* of scary. You will laugh and you will scare, but its not definitively tied to these qualities. What it's really bound to is its intrigue. It's *very* intriguing. It is wrapped up in multiple mysteries and people's personal stories that intersect at a single point - something that may or may not even exist. 

These mundane personal stories drive the comedy and the sadness of our man duo, Mark and Sean. Their back-and-forths are the car AC set to max cool in an otherwise suffocating, tense, atmosphere. Awkward and stilted at times, but it works on that personal and atmospheric level because the game earns your attention and interest to where you're theorizing on what is said as much as what isn't. Admittedly, by the end, Marcus' reactions to objects and other interactables does not suggest the danger and dread warranted by the locale. Its a small gripe, and one that admittedly adds the unsettling, confusing mood of the game. It can be spun that way purely because so many other choices in the game are clearly intentional and well done.

The game is always throwing something new at you: a new piece of the puzzle to either Mark's personal story or the conspiracy he's chasing, a new place to explore and survive(?), or a new piece of litter to pick up (I enjoyed this on a personal level). But seriously, you can't really predict where you're going to go and when. You can't know what someone is going to look like before they're introduced. It is incredible that its foreshadowing can leave you so in the dark despite itself, while still making sense. One of the saddest and most evocative things about this game, to me, came from nothing spoken or played, but portrayed - how a single character was abstracted in the eyes of Mark. 

We cycle through a web of interconnected themes: family, death, falling out of love, friendship, fatherhood, dreams, conspiracy, isolation... they come at you with a seemingly unsorted cadence that translates into something that makes sense. Maybe it'd be better to call it a roller coaster with a lot of flashing lights? Yet its a pro rather than a con that I find it so difficult to pin down exactly why the story hits so hard. If I had to give an answer, it would be that every scene is strong and every area is interesting. Camera direction plays a huge part in this, and its present in the incredible fixed angles during gameplay and the chosen ones in cutscenes. 

Divisive is the gameplay, which I found to range from fun to frustrating, trending toward fun. You do a lot of walking, and you can get lost albeit in a limited space. You won't be backtracking like crazy, but if you get really stuck, you can end up spending a lot of time walking the same routes. The tank controls of the game are important, even if a mild nuisance sometimes. During the tense parts of the games, they enhance the anxiety knowing you can't maneuver yourself well, and during the *really* tense parts of the game, that anxiety fits like a glove.

The game does have dull spots, though rare. It does an incredibly good job with its pacing minus [spoiler]the amusement park[/spoiler] where nothing much happens. Truly this is the only deadspot of the game, and even then it is not without its secrets. If you can engage with all the aspects of the game prior to this, then you can take the unwarranted breather that it gives you and hop right back on the roller coaster right straight through to the end. 

10 Dead Doves is one of the most interesting games I've ever played that executes on much of what it sets out to do. It is perhaps too ambitious, but it aimed at the peak and tumbled a bit lower into "amazing". Please give it a big try even if this normally isn't your thing.

I recognize in it a number of tropes that have flowed in and out of vogue- [spoiler] the abandoned park, the urban legends, the silly but vaguely-defined serial killer who disappeared into the woods, the pseudo-government organization, the obscure process by which you can access another world or have a wish granted, the various entities of questionable motive but very alluring design, the side character who seems way more invested in you and your success than the main character is and is far too forgiving of your flaws, the mundane darkness in your soul that spirals out into something bigger [/spoiler], and it all melds together into something charming, entrancing, and overall, fun. Fun to play, fun to think about, fun to toy with mentally. 

It's not perfect. I'm not sure it's thematically cohesive and the plot is fluid and surreal in a way that makes sense in the moment, but seems a little disjointed when you zoom out, and I can't decide if that's intentional or not. There are two endings, and they will be very to taste, and while they aren't bad, I'm not entirely sure either of them fully stick the landing, but the journey is so intriguing, I don't think that really matters. The artstyle is engaging and hits that sweet spot between being really fun and really uncanny, in a very deliberate sense. This is a fairly long review, but doesn't contain spoilers.
-----------------------------------------------------------

I haven't played something like this in a very long time.  

Essentially, 10 Dead Doves is a 3rd person adventure game with lots of horror and mystery stuff going on, but it's continuously surreal through to the very end.  It's like a wild mash-up of a David Cage game, the camera from Alone in the Dark, the dream sequences from Max Payne, the trippy bits from Paratopic, with the jankiness of Deadly Premonition.  I could draw parallels to many other games, but 10 Dead Doves has its own very unique voice.

You play as Marcus Stetson, a supposedly "pathetic" man with a mysterious past, who appears to be going on some kind of self-discovery adventure somewhere in the Appalachians with his buddy Sean.  Marcus looks, and sounds, psychotic most of the time, he stares with intensity with the unusual approach of scanned eyes and faces they use on the characters.  The PS1-style horror graphics are the first thing to hit you, followed by the dialogue which is voiced by the developers.  It mostly works, they've all done a decent job of most voice lines, though some of it can sometimes be a little intense, though this isn't jarring and feels appropriate to the game.  The musical score is excellent throughout, though sometimes the mixing of the voices and music become muddied - my advice, keep subtitles on.

As a horror game, there were times I twitched a bit - there are mild jump-scares, but nothing too horrific or gory.  I loved the creepiness given to the animations of the bogeymen characters that stalk you in the darkness.  The story veers between borderline contrived, to surreal, to dark, with some proper laugh out loud moments as the game pays homage to cinema and other games.  It's never fully clear why you're there, but that's part of the charm.  The devs clearly want to keep you on your toes all the way through, and to say any more would be spoilers.  

Frustrations?  Yeah, there are a few.  The tank controls can be quite cumbersome, and hitting the invisible barriers of the scenery can also annoy, especially when navigating a corridor maze.  It makes a cute little faint trombone sound when you bump up against these, which helps at least.  There's also a lot of walking, and the puzzles are the simple style of _"collect something, use over there"_, but luckily without too much backtracking, most of the time (with the exception of the forest part in the middle).  And I mentioned the dialogue and story can feel contrived, which I think could turn off a lot of players.  There are odd rambling speeches, and attempts at Edgar Allen Poe-style verses that teeter on the brink of sounding like absolute nonsense.

I know some of these criticisms sound quite heavy, but for me, such issues were easily overlooked given the constant depth of surrealism in exploring the environment.  The areas you travel through are often hallucinatory, as you explore both the present world and the dreams and thoughts of Marcus' past.  The way I got through this was to just go with the flow, and see what happens next rather than trying to understand everything - if you take that approach, it becomes a lot more enjoyable.  The sense of going "down the rabbit hole" in this game never ceased to amaze me.  

There is also a kind of "decisions matter" system throughout the game, based on your actions, but I was never quite clear how to influence the scales (represented literally in this game by white & black chess pieces) one way or the other.  Fortunately, you get to make a final decision at the end of the game which I assume overrides everything previously - but I'm not sure.  As there is only one save, and no option to re-load or change to see the other ending, I will have to play the entire game again to find out what the other ending is.  Assuming there are just two endings, that is.

I'm keen to do that.  I'm convinced that there is a depth to this game that I likely haven't appreciated on my first run (which lasted about 10 hours).  I had a few questions in my head at the end which I'm hoping may be answered either by seeing the story again, or via  the "developer commentary" mode.  

So in summary, this is my GOTY 2024.  What an utterly bizarre adventure it is.  It sparked my brain neurons wildly, like wandering around a surrealist/dada-ist art gallery, or watching a Gaspar Noe film.  It won't be for everyone, but it is most definitely for me.

Worth noting though, that these segments did impose the lingering fear that a threat could be around, which made certain sections of the game really shine to me as far as horror and atmosphere goes. These scenes, while having their own unique gimmick to them, wouldn't have worked if I didn't have to play tag with a monster beforehand, so I can accept the kind of horror game this is to get to enjoy some of the horror segments it lated showed off.

There's one singular problem I believe the game has, the voice acting isn't all that great at times, it's pretty amateurish. I understand why this is the case, and I don't believe the VA work is actually *bad* to the point it detracts from the experience in a meaningful way, but I do think some scenes could have been reworked to better deal with the fact that the VA work couldn't make some lines sound as expressive as they should have been.

 [b] The tldr though [/b] is that I do believe that if you're a fan of story focused games, which heavily rely on strong imagery, enjoy atmospheric horror, and likes a bit of poetry. You should play this game.

Fascinating psychological horror indie, a bit Lynchian in its uncanny surrealism, a bit bleak too and a whole lot of ominous. Persistent confusion, cute/ugly PSX-inspired graphics, layers of depth and batteries included. 

This is one of those plots where sometimes drastically different (reality, time, visuals) parts of it are strung together by a loose, barely coherent thread that keeps weaving in and out of sight, and yet it manages to present a player with a compelling narrative, nonetheless. “Compelling” doesn’t equal “discernable”, by the way, or “non ambiguous”. It just means you’ll end up feeling along the lines of “What was this all about?” together with “Ah, never mind, it was quite eerie and fun regardless”. Here’s a fairly straightforward chunk of the story, a tad artistically gritty but with a meaning one can catch. And a moment later, you’re standing in front of the castle talking to statues about their car keys because they need to skip town. One minute you’re in a van with your best friend looking for mysterious Ant Farm, next – you’re sitting over a chess set with a white dove, talking about “Fat Hotline” where you can press a button, depending on whether you want to be more fat or less. You know, the usual. 

It's a narrative-centered game, so the story is king here, and all the creative perplexity aside, it manages to pull off a very decent horror atmosphere. It’s not in-your-face-loud or hard-hitting, but more like a slight buzzing that is always in the back of your head, telling you that something is very wrong here, but you can’t quite understand what. It completes itself with effective environmental scares and imaginative creepy visuals. And while walking and having dialogues and visions would take up most of your time, you also always have a task to accomplish or occasional puzzle to solve. None of it is challenging or, I believe, even meant to be such, and all of it just adds to the overall uneasiness of neither the character you play nor you, the player, knowing what’s going on and being on guard all the time.

The unwieldy controls that you’ll use to navigate through these shenanigans deserve a separate mention. They are tank controls on mushrooms. And, I suppose, it’s a testament to the storytelling that this is a positive review. Masochists, this one's for you.

Visuals that set out to be cinematic don’t help that “controls situation” one bit, as you going to be slammed with a plethora of angles that change every few seconds. Not sure if having that many added anything to the narrative or simply scratched some artistic itch, but I could have done without them trying to control poor Mark. Other than that, trendy PSX aesthetic brings a familiar “so ugly, it’s kinda cute” look only nostalgia can invoke. There are a few visually interesting surrealistic sequences woven into all that retro glory, and for everything 10 Dead Doves has proven to be - it works well for its designed purpose, as the atmosphere stays unnerving throughout the entire journey.

The score is on par as it’s also crosses into “cinematic” and does so successfully, ramping up the tension when needed and doing the mandatory sharp/crazy violin sound indicating tension, you know the one. Voice-over is also top-notch, although it took me a second to get used to slightly nasal tone of Mark, and a bit dorky, on the edge of the flu Sean’s tone. They acted their lines superbly, and so did everyone else no matter how weird (and, boy, it gets weird) the lines and voices themselves happened to be. There’s even a little musical number. I’m still not sure whether I was surprised or not at all, considering the rest of the game.

10 Dead Doves is a quality story-centric horror that would be appreciated more by those who don’t mind philosophical discourse, head-scratching poetry, mind-bending surreal sequences and a solid dose of “figure out yourself what that means, OK?” along with their horror. And the horror part is well-done here, but in order to be savored you’ll need to pick through all that baggage it brought along, and while I found it enjoyable and, at times, confusing, this isn’t your “take my mind off things and just have fun” experience, this is more of “I feel like challenging my brain with unwinding some twisty story I may never fully understand” one. It’s a good one, really, but better suited for certain kinda player or a certain kinda mood

I don't know how to best summarize this game because I don't really feel like I understand everything I saw, but it's DIFFERENT. I've never played anything like it. The visual style is a collage, and so is the gameplay. Mostly you walk around in a fixed perspective, but there's a first-person segment AND a third-person segment. Sometimes you get to make decisions by clicking boxes; something like eight hours in I was ambushed with a stack of quick-time events. All of this is layered over a plot where increasingly strange real-world situations start to blend into the deteriorating mental landscape of the player character. It's both creepy and funny.

I have to stress the overall positive impact because if I just went over details I think I'd nit-pick it to death. The puzzles are sometimes patronizingly complex, and you're not always rewarded for doing them. Example: In one area, I found a decryption key, then found the thing the key decoded, then found the safe the code opened, and... just spent the rest of the game carrying the item I got from the safe. I never found a chance to use it.

Overall, this is a game that's rough around the edges, and at times I felt like the story's reach exceeded its grasp. As the study of a particular set of characters in a specific time and place, it is excellent. Shoutout to the random Discord user whose profile said "Wishlist 10 Dead Doves on Steam" with no context; you led me here.

This is a once-in-a-generation kind of game. If you told me two years ago when I played the demo that I'd experience the range of emotions that I did playing the full game, I would have said, "Wow. That's really specific. Who are you?"
10 Dead Doves scratches an itch in my brain that I didn't know I had. It takes inspiration from a myriad of sources and transforms it into a wholly unique experience. There are not jumpscares, but you will edge around corners, questioning as to whether or not to proceed. You'll find yourself staying up to decrypt ciphers, reading up on obscure literature, and becoming one... with the Ant Farm...
Laughter. Joy. Fear. Anger. I got actually angry at some parts and not because the gameplay was frustrating, but because I wanted to scream at the characters! The gameplay is not incredibly challenging, but presents enough of one that one will be itching to come right back and finish what they started. Not to mention all of the tantalizing secrets and lore scattered throughout. 
I can say with my whole heart what a genuine pleasure it's been to play through this game. I loved the subversion of expectations the same way I loved In Sound Mind's with the humor, followed immediately by me questioning existence itself and the meanings of my dreams. 10 Dead Doves has a permanent place in my heart and brainmeats for all of eternity.

Fans of classic horror games like Silent Hill or fans of narrative games in general should absolutely give 10 Dead Doves a play!

Holy shit, an absolute masterpiece. I would definitely recommend this for any psychological horror connoisseurs. It has the obvious major Silent Hill inspirations, but there's so many pieces of so many other things, and it all comes together as something incredibly original, horrifying, and beautiful. If you're like me and not used to fixed perspective games, don't let that put you off, it's not that hard, you get used to it quick.

You go into 10 Dead Doves thinking it’s a weird little indie game, and you leave feeling like something broke inside you. Even odder is that you start to feel like maybe you needed that breaking. 

This game is a lot. It's an endless back-and-forth between genres, and an amazingly executed one at that. Think road trip comedy to survival horror… to a dozen other modes of artistry. It's layers of dreams upon realities, ad infinitum. It’s also a piecing together of what made someone who they are, like you're holding their memories in your very hands. The memories aren’t ordered, but that’s how they make sense, weirdly enough. That’s what this game feels like. A god weighing the goods and the uglies of the life of his one specific creation.

10 Dead Doves terrifying, but it’s also tender. One second you’re staring at something monstrous and wrong, with uneven eyes in all the wrong places, and the next you realize this weird creature is kind of adorable. The game messes with your perspective like that multiple times, and you’re forced to dwell on how quickly we can rewrite what we see once we know the story/context behind it. Amazing characterization, amazing relationship studies. 

The main characters are just two guys trying to get through something bigger than themselves. They’re funny, they’re flawed, and they're endlessly lovable. Honestly, kudos to the devs for the self inserts – you’ve made fine, fine characters oozing humanity and relatability.

One of, if not, THE best games I've played as of late. The plot, the characters, the style, even the music is all really good. I love how this game looks, the facial animations look a little "odd" at first but I feel like it's perfect for a game like this and I wouldn't have it any other way. The voice acting I thought was top notch, you really feel Mark when he's angry and when he's losing his marbles. He is truly the most pathetic man on earth, just as described. My favorite kinda guy. 

The dynamic between Mark and Sean grew on me. They're fun characters, more so, fun to watch suffer. They bicker and they banter and you'll wonder if they're even friends. But just like everything in this game, their friendship is a trainwreck and it works for them. 

There are a lot of beautiful shots in this game. The surreal environments can be so beautiful in a very abstract kind of way. 

The character designs for some characters are simple but still very interesting. 

And most of all I enjoyed the writing. It's a very well written game with quirky dialogue. It can be really funny when it wants to be, really vague when it needs to be, and very emotional as well. I mean... They have a drink brand called Aloca-Coc, and Jag-offs beef jerky, man. I love to jag-off and have Aloca-Coc! 

Sometimes I like just chilling in the main menu for a bit to enjoy the music. It's a vibe! 

All in all, this game is fantastic and you'd be a fool not to give it a try. It's a treat.

A strange, unique and VERY memorable mix of Lovecraft, Twin Peaks, Stalker (the movie) and Silent Hill. I'm still not sure if what I just played was a magnificent work of art or a bunch of artsy seeming gibberish but I thoroughly enjoyed it either way. I played it once and I will play it again and recommend it to others whenever I can. 

Pros: Presentation is extremely strong. Music is good, graphics look great with good direction and "camera" placement and a strange off kilter feel to everything that is both effectively spooky and humorously absurdist. Atmosphere is excellent as well and the story is told in an intriguing and mysterious way that will hold your interest all the way through and while I'm still not sure I fully understand it, it was very emotionally effective. 

Cons: There are almost no real puzzles in this game. Mostly it's just finding an item and using it on something and they seem to only be there to make you look around at everything. I'd actually say it's more of a visual novel than a real adventure game, though that may be a plus for some. The game's style and writing are very love it or hate it. I loved it but I could see someone holding the opposite opinion. Interacting with objects of interest can sometimes be very fiddly with the player needing to stand in exactly the right place. There is some minor jank. Not a big deal and may be fixed in future patches but it was there when I played it.

In conclusion, if you looked at the description and looked at the trailer and screenshots and thought it looked good then ABSOLUTELY get this game. It's not perfect but it is utterly unique, entertaining, memorable and fascinating. We need more games like this one.

But... this game doesn't seem to know what it wants to be. Is it horror? If so, what kind of horror? Psychological? About urban legends? Or is it suddenly an SCP-style schlock?

It feels like an incomprehensible amalgam of everything. You can't just shove whatever comes into your head into a game and rely on a deus ex machina to justify the lack of story direction. That might be Sam Lake's signature move, but it's becoming painfully stale.

[h3]Style Without Substance[/h3]
Nonsensical events lead to even more nonsensical events. I loved the demo and really wanted to like this, but the writing and gameplay in the full release left me completely cold. It’s just boring and uninteresting. Life’s too short to be running around in some surreal representation of the developer’s psyche, collecting litter and trying to solve puzzles by having to explore every single nook and cranny of the maze-like environments. No thanks.
Game has severe softlock issues, refunded as it seems to be a common problem. Neat game otherwise.

The game was mostly decent up the cabin in the woods part. Interesting story build up, decent exploration and atmosphere, and some okayish light puzzle solving, with some nice horror elements.

But after the cabin, the game loses any semblance of making sense it might have had before, and just starts feeling like a never-endings sequence of boring passageways, mazes, pointless notes and nonsensical babbling. It's like modern developers forgot how to write good horror. When you're placed in a surreal world where physical laws don't really apply and nothing even makes any sense, nothing is surprising or scary anymore. A creepy phone call? Hardly unexpected. A monster chasing you? Sure, what's new...

I guess having a story break into a complete nonsense by the end is becoming rather commonplace in horror games. Remember when Fahrenheit/Indigo Prophecy ended up throwing all kind of crap at the end of the game, resulting in a rather disappointing ending after the good build-up in the first part? Seems like modern horror developers continue that trend and try to outmatch each other at how ridiculous and insane can they turn their story into, and it's honestly a trend I'm getting very tired of.

Hell, near the end of this game, you encounter a character who says "Artists today try too hard to be groundbreaking, instead of actually trying to be good" or something along these lines. I think this relates perfectly to the writing of this game. Why not focus on one thing and try to write a good horror story around it, instead of throwing everything you can think of inside and making your game feel like one of those "art films" that GTA5 makes fun of in it's in-game theatres, and pretend that this somehow makes the story deep and meaningful, rather than vague and nonsensical.

There's nothing wrong with taking ideas and inspirations from other media. But at least give them some purpose and focus. So far I've noticed influences from other horror movies and games like Saw, Slender Man, Until Dawn, A Cabin In The Woods, and there are probably others I haven't picked up. Some of them make sense, but did we really need a first-person segment that plays exactly like Slender man and 8 notes or whatever it was called? That was honestly just a bloat, and the game is filled with the bloat in it's last third. Another maze I have to trudge through using the tank controls? Oh, now there's a stealth segment INSIDE a maze!? And a maze after that??? How is that supposed to be any fun!?

This makes me so sad. The game is full of brave visual choices and some interesting monster design, with an interesting, specific setting, but for a narrative-led title there is a drastic lack of interesting story beats or character development. I think this story could have been told well, with an interesting twist and motive reveal... but in about half the playtime.

I do appreciate the fixed multicam work, I dig the occasional switches to first person and OTS in order to change up the tone and atmosphere. The animated faces are entertaining and the cinematography is workable.

...

I dig cryptic approaches to narrative, and I can enjoy a story that takes it's time explaining itself... but usually you need to have some kind of charismatic lead(s) or strong plot hook, neither of which are deployed at the beginning of this game. By the time the overwrought and hackneyed cosmogony of the world was explained, I was thoroughly disinterested in what happened to these leaden protagonists.

I mean, it turns out one guy is a REAL asshole! Which is fine as a twist! But by the point it's revealed I really didn't care about him, his friend, their lives - the characters as drawn felt utterly charmless to me. There's not enough story here to justify the screen time. This game desperately needed a ruthless script editor.

Can the gameplay save it? Not really. Some exciting chases and a couple of puzzles spice up listless exploration and a procession of dire mazes, some missing any interesting landmarks to make them bearable.

I really, really wanted to like this, but it wasn't for me. Again, I can recommend it on a purely visual spectrum,  but if you find yourself getting bored over the runtime of this game, I urge you to abandon ship - it will not get more interesting.

A real shame. I hope Duonix gets to make a follow-up game - but ideally something MUCH shorter.

This game is obviously a passion project and I really liked the beginning of the game when it's two friends with good chemistry solving a mystery, but then it goes completely off the rails. Maybe I just don't get Lynchian storytelling as there was pretty much no point I could follow what was happening. Most of the game is a series of disconnected scenes with melodramatic heavy handed writing. More incoherent than deep.
